pages.x: Around 1250 BC the eastern Mediterranean was shared by great kingdoms whose kings wrote to each other as brothers: Egypt, the Hittites, Babylon, Assyria and the Mycenaean Greeks. Ships carried copper from Cyprus and tin from as far as Afghanistan to make bronze. One wreck, found off Turkey at Uluburun, carried ten tonnes of copper.

In the decades after 1200 BC nearly all of it vanished. The Hittite capital Hattusa was burned and abandoned. The palaces of Mycenae and Pylos fell, and Greece forgot how to write for 400 years. In the rich port of Ugarit, letters begging for ships and soldiers were found where they had been left, perhaps never sent.

Egyptian records blame raiders from the sea, peoples on the move with their families. Around 1175 BC Ramesses III fought them in the Nile Delta and won, and had the battle carved on the walls of his temple at Medinet Habu. The Philistines may have been one of these peoples.

Historians now think no single cause was to blame. Drought and famine, earthquakes, revolts, raiders and the breakdown of trade may all have struck together, and because the kingdoms depended on each other, the fall of one dragged down the next.

Smaller peoples grew in the space left behind: the Phoenicians, who spread an alphabet of just 22 letters, the Israelites, the Arameans and the Philistines. Iron, found almost everywhere, replaced bronze, which needed tin carried from far away.

The collapse ended the Bronze Age world and opened the Iron Age. Out of the dark centuries that followed came the alphabet, the Greece of Homer and the kingdom of Israel. Historians study it as a warning of how a connected world can fall apart all at once.
pts: Ended the great kingdoms of the Bronze Age
Greece forgot how to write for 400 years
Made way for iron and the alphabet
